note: The closed vocabulary for `durableStores[].corruptionPolicy` in governance/store-recoverability.v1.json, plus the count ratchet on that register. It lives in a SEPARATE file on purpose: the register's rows change often and in parallel with other lanes, and a vocabulary edit landing in the same file as a row edit is a merge conflict for no reason. Every other enumerated answer in that register (owner, recoverability, status, upgradeHandling, root, pathVerification, encryption) is already a closed Set in scripts/ci/check-store-recoverability.mjs; corruptionPolicy was the one answer still free text, so 'what happens to the user's bytes when this file is unreadable' was the only question a row could answer with a spelling nobody else uses. This file is NOT read at runtime by either register consumer (modules/shell/src-tauri/src/updater.rs, modules/ui UpgradeReconciliationProbe) - it is a build-time vocabulary only.
extensionProcedure: A genuinely new corruption behaviour is a legitimate reason to extend this file. Add the value here WITH its one-line meaning in the same commit as the row that uses it, and make the meaning describe the OBSERVABLE outcome for the user's bytes (kept / rewritten / deleted / refused), not the implementation. Do not add a near-synonym of an existing value to avoid editing a row: 26 values for 36 rows is already close to one-per-row, so another that means the same as one of these is drift, not precision. If a new value would be a synonym, reuse the existing one and say the difference in the row's corruptionNote instead. A value with no row is normally a FAILURE (the gate says so), because a vocabulary that only grows becomes a list of spellings nobody uses. The ONE exception is a value declared ahead of a row landing in a different in-flight branch: put it in `awaitingRow` as { reason, until }, where `reason` names a PR (`#613`) or branch (`worktree-<name>`) and `until` is an ISO date. It retires on BOTH paths, which is the point: if the row lands the gate fails while the marker is still there, and if the PR is abandoned the gate fails once `until` passes. An expiry-less marker would only have retired on success, so an abandoned PR would have made the value permanent.

policies.ACTIVE_AND_FUTURE_LOGS_FAIL_LOUD: An unreadable or future-versioned active journal is an error, not a skipped line; the process refuses rather than continuing against state it cannot read.
policies.CLASSIFY_UNCLEAN_AND_REGENERATE: An unreadable entry is classified as unclean and regenerated from its source; nothing user-authored is at stake.
policies.CONSERVATIVE_REBUILD_OR_CLEAR: A damaged marker is rebuilt if it can be, and otherwise cleared, choosing the conservative outcome over trusting partial bytes.
policies.DELETE_AND_RECOMPUTE: A damaged snapshot is ignored and overwritten by the next write; derived progress bookkeeping that does carry the last enumerated path. NAME/BEHAVIOUR MISMATCH, kept visible rather than smoothed over: nothing deletes this file — MigrationProgressStore.readBestEffort swallows the parse failure at debug and returns null (modules/worker-core/src/main/java/io/justsearch/indexerworker/index/MigrationProgressStore.java:56-59), and the write path replaces it via ATOMIC_MOVE (:91-99). Renaming the value is a register-row edit, so it belongs to the row's owner, not to this vocabulary.
policies.DISCARD_UNREADABLE_DERIVED_STATUS_AND_RE: Unreadable derived status is discarded and re-derived by a fresh scan rather than repaired in place.
policies.FAIL_CLOSED: The operation stops. Nothing is written, nothing is overwritten, and the caller is told it cannot proceed.
policies.FAIL_CLOSED_AND_RETRY_PREPARATION: The operation stops and the preparation step is retried from the beginning rather than resumed from unreadable state.
policies.FAIL_CLOSED_DISABLED_WRITE_LOCKED: The operation stops and the feature stays disabled with the store write-locked, so a corrupt file cannot be silently replaced by a default that re-enables it.
policies.FAIL_CLOSED_REPAIR_REQUIRED: The operation stops and stays stopped until an explicit repair; the process will not choose a recovery on the user's behalf.
policies.FAIL_LOUD: The read refuses instead of returning empty or default state, and the bytes are left exactly as they are. HETEROGENEOUS ACROSS ITS THREE ROWS, stated rather than averaged: ai-install-contract and encryption-keystore genuinely THROW (InstallContractIO.read raises CorruptDurableStoreException at InstallContractIO.java:41,:53; EncryptionKeystore.load lets Jackson's exception escape and calls StoreFormatVersions.requireReadable, EncryptionKeystore.java:36-46). user-policy does NOT throw: EnterprisePolicyServiceImpl catches, logs a warning and returns PolicyLoad(present=true, loaded=false, <message>) — the field is `loaded`, not `valid` (:265) — and an unsupported schemaVersion returns the same shape (:283-285). What happens next differs by path and is worth stating: an unloadable MACHINE policy fails CLOSED (:73-86 disables downloads, online AI and GPU and sets disallowExternalInferenceServers, because a tampered policy must not silently permit everything), while the surrounding effective policy otherwise starts from PERMISSIVE defaults (:66-69) and only narrows them (:100-106). The common guarantee across all three rows is 'never silently substituted with a default, never rewritten', not 'an exception is thrown'.
policies.FAIL_LOUD_AND_PRESERVE: Reading raises a visible error AND the unreadable bytes are preserved untouched, because they are user-authored and may still be recoverable by hand.
policies.FAIL_LOUD_ON_UNREADABLE_OR_FUTURE_LINE: A line that is unreadable OR written by a newer schema aborts the whole read rather than being skipped, so a downgrade cannot silently drop entries: NdjsonAppendStore.readAll lets the Jackson parse escape and throws IOException / UnsupportedStoreVersionException per line (NdjsonAppendStore.java:100-118). Two non-corruption exceptions to 'you always see everything', stated so the guarantee is not read as wider than it is: blank lines are skipped (:100-102), and a sealed store that is currently LOCKED returns an empty list rather than failing (:95-97).
policies.FAIL_OR_REBUILD_DERIVED_QUEUE: A corrupt queue either fails loudly or is rebuilt from the durable source it derives from; queued work is never silently lost without one of the two happening.
policies.NEVER_DELETE_OR_OVERWRITE_UNKNOWN_ASSET: An asset the app does not recognise is never deleted or overwritten; it belongs to the user and is left in place regardless of what the app expected to find.
policies.PRESERVE_AND_RECOVER_DEFAULTS: The unparseable file is moved aside under a distinct name (UiSettingsStore.quarantineCorruptFile :198, with a non-atomic fallback at :200), defaults are loaded, and the recovery is surfaced as a condition — the user keeps the old bytes and is told. If the move itself fails the original exception is rethrown with the IO failure suppressed into it (:202-204), so defaults are never loaded WITHOUT preserving.
policies.RECOVER_PREVIOUS_OR_REBUILD: The previous good generation is recovered if one exists; otherwise the store is rebuilt from source.
policies.RECREATE_DERIVED_METRIC: The metric file is recreated from scratch; it holds only derived measurements.
policies.REFUSE_FUTURE_SCHEMA_AND_PRESERVE_OVERRI: A future schema version is refused rather than downgraded, and any user overrides in the file are preserved rather than rewritten.
policies.REGENERATE_BEFORE_CONSUMPTION: The snapshot is regenerated before anything reads it, so a stale or damaged copy is never consumed.
policies.REGENERATE_FROM_RUN_EVENTS_OR_PRESERVE: A missing or unreadable derived artifact is regenerated from the owning run's terminal events at boot and on key unlock; when it cannot be regenerated — a locked store, for instance — the bytes are preserved, never dropped.
policies.REGENERATE_OR_DROP_DERIVED_HISTORY: Derived history is regenerated where possible and otherwise dropped; losing it costs a recomputation, not user content.
policies.ROTATE_OR_PRUNE_DIAGNOSTIC_ARTIFACT: The damaged diagnostic artifact is rotated away or pruned rather than repaired; losing it costs only diagnosability. Note what it holds while it exists: NOT content-free — the row's own encryptionNote records that exported span attributes include doc.path and http.target, so indexed document paths and request query strings land in telemetry/*.ndjson, and crashes/*.json keeps raw exception messages and stack traces.
policies.SKIP_DERIVED_ROW: An unreadable row is skipped and the rest of the dataset is used; the set is regenerable from the source documents, so no single row is load-bearing. Content caveat: the rows ARE user-derived — each carries a synthetic query generated from one of the user's own documents plus that document's id.
policies.SKIP_INVALID_PLUGIN_AND_PRESERVE_BYTES: An invalid plugin payload is skipped rather than loaded, and its bytes are preserved rather than deleted — the payload is the user's.
policies.SKIP_UNREADABLE_LINE_AND_WARN: An unreadable journal line is skipped rather than losing every later entry to one bad line. TWO honest qualifications on 'and warn': only a line that fails to PARSE warns (ActionEventJournal.parseLine :268-271); a line that parses but is structurally invalid — missing id or kind, unparseable occurredAt — is dropped SILENTLY by ActionLedgerProjection.fromWireRow returning Optional.empty (:264-266, :272-274). And the skip is per-line, not per-file: Files.readAllLines sits outside the try at ActionEventJournal.java:254, so an IO failure there aborts that generation and the remaining generations with it.
policies.VERIFY_HASH_OR_PRESERVE_USER_ASSET: The asset is accepted only if its hash verifies; a mismatch preserves the user's file rather than replacing it.
policies.VERIFY_PROCESS_IDENTITY_OR_REPLACE_STALE: A lock is honoured only if the owning process still exists; a lock left by a dead process is replaced rather than waited on forever.

ratchet.note: Two numbers, both pinned OUTSIDE the register they describe. Before this, `pendingDurableClassification.cap` called itself 'a ratchet' while living in the same file as the entries it capped, so one commit could add a pending entry and raise the cap that forbade it. `durableStoreRows` is a FLOOR, not an equality: rows are meant to be added (that is the register growing to cover more of the tree), and a lane adding rows in parallel must not red this gate. A row DISAPPEARING is the event worth a build failure — a durable authority does not stop existing quietly.
ratchet.remedy: If a durable store is genuinely retired, lower `durableStoreRows` here in the same commit that removes its row, and say in the commit message where its bytes went. If the pending list genuinely needs more room, raise `pendingDurableClassificationCap` here AND in the register, and add a `bumps` entry saying which store forced it and what its blocker is. Never raise the cap to make a new pending entry fit without both.

retirements.lane: lane F stage A item A19 (tempdoc 936)
retirements.whereItsBytesWent: Nowhere — the file stopped being written and nothing reads it. It was <dataDir>/runtime/worker-config-snapshot.json, the Head's resolved configuration serialised for a SECOND JVM to load at config ordinal 450. Items A11/A13 deleted that JVM, so the store had one writer and no reader; A19 deleted the writer (HeadlessApp), the ordinal-450 tier, ResolvedConfig.toWorkerSnapshot/loadWorkerSnapshot and ResolvedConfigBuilder.contributeWorkerSnapshot/loadWorkerSnapshotFromSysprop/loadRawWorkerSnapshotFromSysprop. There is one ResolvedConfig in one JVM now, so there are no bytes to relocate: the data still exists, in memory, as the object both halves already share. An existing installation keeps a stale file on disk that nothing opens; it is inert, not orphaned state, and no migration is required.
